sections.title: WHAT IS A GRAND PRIX CIRCUIT?

slides.title: Racing circuit concept
content: A Grand Prix circuit is a controlled road-course environment engineered for high-speed competition, timing, officiating and emergency response.
Formula 1 uses both permanent facilities and temporary/street venues; geometry strongly influences car setup, tyres, overtaking and risk.

slides.title: FIA recognition and homologation
content: FIA circuit recognition is the formal process used to assess a circuit for competition. Formula 1 venues require the applicable FIA grading and event approval.

Recognition covers geometry, protection, runoff, medical and rescue capability, marshals, access, paddock and other safety considerations; exact requirements depend on the circuit grade and regulations.

slides.title: Core infrastructure
rows: Controlled area for pit stops and team servicing
Additional recovery/deceleration space outside the racing surface
Contain/redirect vehicles and absorb or manage crash energy
Define track edge and influence car placement
Observe, signal and respond to incidents
Enable rapid treatment, rescue and extraction

events.event: Grand Prix racing develops on long public-road and temporary courses.
Permanent facilities expand while long road circuits remain important.
Formula 1 World Championship begins.

slides.title: From road courses to permanent facilities
content: Historic circuits such as the original Spa and Nürburgring used long public-road sections with limited separation from fixed hazards. Permanent facilities enabled more controlled runoff, barriers, marshal access, pit areas and spectator infrastructure.
Circuit design gradually became an engineered safety system rather than simply a measured road route.

events.event: Runoff, catch fencing, medical response and barrier development become increasingly central.
Many historic circuits are shortened, reprofiled or removed from F1 as safety expectations rise.
Homologation, energy-absorbing barriers, runoff design and advanced medical systems become integral to modern venue planning.

slides.title: Why a venue's history needs event context
content: A circuit can have a long history without every event being a Formula 1 World Championship race. This database separates first use, non-championship F1 events, World Championship events and later returns.
The same site can also have several configurations, so statistics should be tied to the relevant layout and event definition.

slides.title: What makes a street circuit
content: Street circuits use public roads, semi-public roads or temporarily configured urban roads. Fixed buildings, drainage, utility covers, limited runoff and existing kerbs constrain circuit geometry.
Temporary construction must also integrate barriers, fencing, pit infrastructure, marshal posts and emergency access into an urban environment.

slides.title: Permanent-circuit engineering
content: Permanent venues integrate fixed runoff, barriers, timing loops, medical facilities, service roads, race control, garages and spectator systems.
They can support several layouts or racing categories without rebuilding the entire venue.

slides.title: Examples of design flexibility
rows: Extensive runoff and many possible configurations
Multiple identities within the broader venue, including the modern GP circuit and Nordschleife
Grand Prix road course beside surviving historic banking
Wide purpose-built track with long straights and large-radius corners

slides.title: Setup consequences
content: Technical circuits reward mechanical balance, traction and precise rotation. Errors in a linked corner sequence can compound into the following corner or straight.
At wall-lined venues such as Monaco and Singapore, small errors can become race-ending incidents because recovery space is limited.

slides.title: Asphalt, aggregate and grip
content: Grip depends on aggregate properties, binder, surface texture, tyre rubber, temperature and wear. Roughness can raise mechanical grip but also increase tyre energy and degradation.
Resurfacing can significantly change track behaviour because new asphalt may be smoother, more or less abrasive, less rubbered-in and differently porous.

events.effect: Little rubber on the racing line; grip may be lower.
Repeated running cleans and rubbers-in the line.
Grip can approach a local weekend peak, depending on temperature and support-category activity.
Rubber, tyre pickup, weather and traffic continue changing grip.
Water film changes friction, drainage and the usable racing line; standing water can become a hydroplaning risk.

slides.title: Weather effects
rows: Changes cooling needs and ambient operating conditions
Strong influence on tyre warm-up, grip and degradation
Reduces grip and changes line/tyre choice
Changes aerodynamic balance and braking/corner-entry confidence
Affects thermal load and drying rate
Reduces air density, altering cooling, drag and downforce

slides.title: Weather-sensitive venues
regions: Weather can vary rapidly across the circuit

slides.title: Emergency infrastructure
items: Debris fencing and controlled access gates

slides.title: FIA homologation and layered safety
content: Circuit safety is a layered system. Homologation evaluates the relationship between track geometry, barriers, runoff, fencing, marshal coverage, medical systems and emergency access.
The exact device mix is venue- and regulation-specific; this database does not assert the presence of a specific barrier system unless a cited source verifies it.

slides.title: Barrier and runoff concepts
items: Guardrails and concrete barriers where appropriate
Tyre barriers or other approved systems where appropriate
TecPro-type systems only where venue documentation verifies use

slides.title: Medical, extraction and marshal operations
content: Incident response depends on rapid recognition, trained marshals, signalling and communications. Rescue crews require practical access routes and extraction capability; serious incidents can require specialist medical response and controlled scene management.
Safety performance therefore depends on the whole circuit operation, not only the visible barrier or runoff.

slides.title: DRS, safety-car and pit-lane effects
content: DRS can influence overtaking on designated straight sections, but the number and location of DRS zones are event-specific and can change.

Safety-car sensitivity is influenced by walls, runoff, incident density and recovery difficulty. Pit-lane time loss depends on pit-entry geometry, pit-lane speed, entry/exit location and the number of laps affected by a stop.

slides.title: Record-quality rules
content: A record must be tied to a source, configuration and statistic definition. Qualifying and race laps must never be merged; old and new layouts must not be treated as one timing environment without a clear scope.
Historical event counts derived from inclusive year sequences are labelled derived rather than presented as independently published statistics.

slides.title: Corner-learning framework
content: Study every corner through approach speed, braking point, turn-in, apex, minimum speed, exit kerb, traction demand and downstream consequence.
A corner is strategically important not only because of its speed but because its exit can set up the next braking zone or straight.

slides.title: Classification methodology
content: These labels are educational classifications, not official FIA circuit grades. They summarise physical geometry and typical vehicle-performance demands described by circuit/F1 material.
A venue can belong to multiple categories simultaneously.

slides.title: 2026 verification snapshot
content: The official live 2026 F1 calendar visible on September 13, 2026 lists 23 scheduled rounds. Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were removed from their original April slots; Bahrain's event was preserved at Sepang as the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia on October 2–4, while Saudi Arabia has no 2026 replacement in the live calendar.

Madrid's event is scheduled for September 11–13, 2026. This database intentionally leaves Madring race-result fields blank until an official result is available in the referenced calendar/race source.
